concepts.name: ECS task role vs task execution role

questions.prompt: Your chat UI must show LLM tokens as they are generated by a model call inside a LangGraph node. Which `stream_mode` gives you that?

choices.text: `"updates"`, which streams each node's state update after it runs
`"values"`, which streams the graph's full state after every step
`"messages"`, which streams (token, metadata) pairs from LLM calls
`"debug"`, which streams each LLM token along with checkpoint data

questions.explanation: `messages` mode streams 2-tuples of an LLM token (or message chunk) and metadata about the node and call, which is what a typing effect needs. `updates` and `values` only arrive after a step finishes, and `debug` combines checkpoint and task events, not tokens.

sources.title: Streaming
sources.claim: Stream modes: `values` (full state after each step), `updates` (state updates after each step), `messages` ((LLM token, metadata) tuples from LLM calls), `custom` (data emitted from nodes or tools with `get_stream_writer`), `checkpoints`, `tasks`, and `debug` (combines checkpoints and tasks with extra metadata).

questions.prompt: You compile a LangGraph graph with `cache=InMemoryCache()` and give an expensive node `cache_policy=CachePolicy()` with no arguments. When does the node reuse a cached result?

choices.text: Never, until you also give it a `ttl`, as caching is off without one
For any input on the same thread, until that thread is deleted
Only within one run, as the cache is cleared when the run ends
When it gets the same input again; with no `ttl`, it never expires

questions.explanation: The default cache key is a hash of the node's input, so the same input hits the cache. `ttl` is optional: without one, entries never expire. Caching is keyed by input, not by thread or run.

sources.title: Graph API overview (LangGraph, Python)
sources.claim: Node caching needs a cache passed when compiling the graph and a `CachePolicy` on the node; `key_func` builds the cache key from the node's input and defaults to a pickle hash of the input, and `ttl` is the time to live in seconds, with no expiry if it is not set.

questions.prompt: Your `agent-api` task on ECS Fargate pulls its image from a private ECR repository, logs to CloudWatch, gets an API key from Secrets Manager through the task definition, and reads documents from S3 at runtime. Which permissions go on the task execution role and which on the task role, and why?

model_answer.summary: The task execution role is for the ECS and Fargate agents that start the task (image pull, logs, injected secrets); the task role is for your application code (S3 reads). Keeping them apart is least privilege.
key_points: The task execution role is used by the ECS container and Fargate agents, and the containers can't use its credentials
It needs ECR pull, CloudWatch Logs (`awslogs`) and `secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` for the secret injected through the task definition
The task role's credentials are given to the application code in the container, so `s3:GetObject` goes there
Keeping them separate, with a role per service, gives each the minimum it needs

questions.explanation: Interviewers ask this because it is a common source of AccessDenied errors. The agent that starts your task and the code inside it are different principals: a secret injected as an environment variable is fetched by the agent before your code runs, while an S3 call from your code uses the task role.

sources.title: Amazon ECS task execution IAM role
sources.claim: The task execution role lets the ECS container and Fargate agents make AWS calls, such as pulling private ECR images, sending logs with `awslogs`, and fetching Secrets Manager or Parameter Store values referenced in the task definition; its credentials aren't directly accessible to the containers.

sources.title: Amazon ECS task IAM role
sources.claim: The task IAM role's permissions are vended to the containers so application code can call AWS services such as S3; they aren't used by the ECS container and Fargate agents. On Fargate, EC2 instance profiles aren't available to containers.

questions.prompt: A tool running inside a LangGraph node should report progress, like "fetched 3 of 10 pages", to the client while it works. How do you do it?

choices.text: Append progress notes to state so `"messages"` mode sends them
Log them, since `"debug"` mode streams every log line a node writes
Call `get_stream_writer()`, then stream with `"custom"` mode
Return them early from the node with `Command(goto=END)` each time

questions.explanation: `get_stream_writer()` gives nodes and tools a writer for custom data, which reaches the client when you stream with `stream_mode="custom"`. `messages` mode carries LLM tokens, and `debug` carries checkpoint and task events, not your logs.

questions.prompt: A cached LangGraph node's input includes a `requested_at` timestamp that changes on every call, so the cache never hits. What fixes it?

choices.text: Give `CachePolicy` a `key_func` that keys on only the fields that matter
Set a much longer `ttl`, so that older entries stay in the cache for longer
Run the graph with `durability="sync"` so the cache is written first
Add a reducer to `requested_at` so caching ignores changes to that key

questions.explanation: The default cache key is a hash of the whole input, so a field that always changes makes every key new. A `key_func` that builds the key from the meaningful fields fixes it. A longer `ttl` keeps entries around but can't make a new key match an old one.

questions.prompt: Code in your Fargate container calls `s3.get_object` and gets AccessDenied, though the task execution role allows `s3:GetObject`. Why?

choices.text: S3 calls from Fargate need a VPC endpoint before any role applies
App code uses the task role; execution role keys go to the agent
Role changes only apply after the container image is rebuilt
Fargate tasks call S3 through the EC2 instance profile instead

questions.explanation: The task execution role's credentials are for the ECS and Fargate agents, and aren't accessible to the containers. Your code uses the task role, so `s3:GetObject` belongs there. On Fargate, EC2 instance profiles aren't available to containers at all.

questions.prompt: Your `agent-api` task on ECS Fargate pulls its image from private ECR, logs with `awslogs`, injects a Secrets Manager key through the task definition, and reads S3 at runtime. Which permissions belong on the task execution role? Select all that apply.

choices.text: Pulling the image from the private ECR repository
`s3:GetObject` for the documents the app reads
Writing container logs to CloudWatch with `awslogs`
`secretsmanager:GetSecretValue` for the injected key
Every AWS call the app's code makes, as a fallback

questions.explanation: The task execution role is used by the ECS container and Fargate agents to start the task: pulling private ECR images (a), sending logs with `awslogs` (c) and fetching Secrets Manager values referenced in the task definition (d). Its credentials aren't available to your containers, so it can't be a fallback for the app (e). The application's own calls, like reading S3 (b), go on the task role, whose credentials are vended to the containers.

sources.title: Amazon ECS task execution IAM role
sources.claim: The task execution role lets the ECS container and Fargate agents make AWS calls such as pulling private ECR images, sending logs with `awslogs` and retrieving Secrets Manager secrets referenced in the task definition; its credentials aren't directly accessible by the containers.

sources.title: Amazon ECS task IAM role
sources.claim: The task IAM role's permissions are vended to the containers so application code can use services such as Amazon S3; they aren't used by the ECS container and Fargate agents.
